They were quite disappointed in the confidences they made choice of; so the prophet tells them they should be: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be ashamed of Egypt,</hi> which thou now trustest in, as formerly <hi type="italic">thou wast of Assyria, who distressed them and helped them not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.20">2 Chron. xxviii. 20</reference>. The Jews were a peculiar people in their profession of religion, and for that reason none of the neighbouring nations cared for them, nor could heartily love them; and yet the Jews were still courting them, and confiding in them, and were well enough served when deceived by them. See what will come of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt go forth from him,</hi> thy ambassadors or envoys shall return from Egypt <hi type="italic">re infectâ—disappointed,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">with their hands upon their heads,</hi> lamenting the desperate condition of their people. Or, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt go forth hence,</hi> that is, into captivity in a strange land, <hi type="italic">with thy hands upon thy head,</hi> holding it because it aches (<hi type="italic">ubi dolor ibi digitus—where the pain is the finger will be applied</hi>), or as people ashamed, for Tamar, in the height of her confusion, <hi type="italic">laid her hand on her head,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.19">2 Sam. xiii. 19</reference>. "And Egypt, that thou reliest on, shall not be able to prevent it nor to rescue thee out of captivity." Those that will not lay their hand on their heart in godly sorrow, which works life, shall be made to lay their hand on their head in the sorrow of the world, which works death. And no wonder that Egypt cannot help them, when God will not, If the Lord do not help thee, whence should I? The Egyptians are broken reeds, for <hi type="italic">the Lord has rejected thy confidences;</hi> he will not make use of them for thy relief, will neither so far honour them, nor so far give countenance to thy confidence in them, as to appoint them to be the instruments of any good to thee, and therefore <hi type="italic">thou shalt not prosper in them;</hi> they shall not stand thee in any stead nor give thee any satisfaction. As <hi type="italic">there is no counsel or wisdom</hi> that can prevail against the Lord, so there is none that can prevail without him. Some read it, <hi type="italic">The Lord has rejected thee for thy confidences;</hi> because thou hast dealt so unfaithfully with him as to trust in his creatures, nay, in his enemies when thou shouldst have trusted in him only, he has abandoned thee to that destruction from which thou thoughtest thus to shelter thyself; and then thou <hi type="italic">canst not prosper,</hi> for none ever either hardened himself against God or estranged himself from God and prospered.  <chapter eID="Jer.2"/> <div eID="gen17198" type="x-p"/>

entries.2052bad3a589af8afb1632873a41c629e6eb137e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9590"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.2.1-Jer.2.37">Jr 2:1-37</reference>. Expostulation with the Jews, Reminding Them of Their Former Devotedness, and God's Consequent Favor, and a Denunciation of God's Coming Judgments for Their Idolatry.</title> <div sID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> Probably in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.2">Jr 1:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jr 3:6</reference>, "also ... in ... days of Josiah"). The warning not to rely as they did on Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jr 2:18</reference>), was in accordance with Josiah's policy, who took part with Assyria and Babylon against Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>). Jeremiah, doubtless, supported the reformation begun by Josiah, in the previous year (the twelfth of his reign), and fully carried out in the eighteenth.<div eID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9590"/><hi type="bold">2. cry--</hi>proclaim.<div eID="gen16838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>the headquarters and center of their idolatry; therefore addressed first.<div eID="gen16839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thee--</hi>rather, "I remember in regard to thee" [Henderson]; "for thee" [Maurer].<div eID="gen16840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kindness of thy youth--</hi>not so much Israel's kindness towards God, as the kindness which Israel experienced from God in their early history (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">Eze 16:8</reference>, 22, 60; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.3">23:3</reference>, 8, 19; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Ho 2:15</reference>). For Israel from the first showed perversity rather than kindness towards God (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.14.11">Ex 14:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.24">15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.1-Exod.32.7">32:1-7</reference>, &c.). The greater were God's favors to them from the first, the fouler was their ingratitude in forsaking Him (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jr 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen16841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">espousals--</hi>the intervals between Israel's betrothal to God at the exodus from Egypt, and the formal execution of the marriage contract at Sinai. Ewald takes the "kindness" and "love" to be Israel's towards God at first (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">Ex 19:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.3">24:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.20-Exod.35.29">35:20-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.36.5">36:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.16-Josh.24.17">Jos 24:16-17</reference>). But compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.16">De 32:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.5">Eze 16:5</reference>, 6, 15, 22 ("days of thy youth") implies that the love here meant was on God's side, not Israel's.<div eID="gen16842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou wentest after me in ... wilderness--</hi>the next act of God's love, His leading them in the desert without needing any strange god, such as they since worshipped, to help Him (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.7">De 2:7</reference>; 32:12). <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference> shows it is God's "leading" of them, not their following after God in the wilderness, which is implied. <div eID="gen16843" type="x-p"/>
entries.44a5bda2d0a22a8166ea975023a4aa7c20c8742c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9591"/><div sID="gen16844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9591"/><hi type="bold">3. holiness unto the Lord--</hi>that is, was consecrated to the service of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">6</reference>). They thus answered to the motto on their high priest's breastplate, "Holiness to the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.6">De 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.2">14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.14.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen16844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first-fruits of his increase--</hi>that is, of Jehovah's produce. As the first-fruits of the whole produce of the land were devoted to God (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Ex 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.18.12">Nu 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.18.13">13</reference>), so Israel was devoted to Him as the first-fruit and representative nation among all nations. So the spiritual Israel (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour--</hi>carrying on the image of first-fruits which were eaten before the Lord by the priests as the Lord's representatives; all who ate (injured) Jehovah's first-fruits (Israel), contracted guilt: for example, Amalek, the Amorites, &c., were extirpated for their guilt towards Israel.<div eID="gen16846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall come--</hi>rather, "came." <div eID="gen16847" type="x-p"/>
entries.20e2c44ff17b3ec9003ce325c5da16ed225ed2d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9592"/><div sID="gen16848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9592"/><hi type="bold">4. Jacob ... Israel--</hi>the whole nation.<div eID="gen16848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">families--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.1.15">Jr 1:15</reference>). Hear God's word not only collectively, but individually (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.12-Zech.12.14">Zec 12:12-14</reference>). <div eID="gen16849" type="x-p"/>
entries.c47d6e9afd3be515697e57d05506b298639f8371: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9593"/><div sID="gen16850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9593"/><hi type="bold">5. iniquity--</hi>wrong done to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Is 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mi 6:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">De 32:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked after vanity--</hi>contrasted with "walkest after me in the wilderness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>): then I was their guide in the barren desert; now they take idols as their guides.<div eID="gen16851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanity ... vain--</hi>An idol is not only vain (impotent and empty), but vanity itself. Its worshippers acquire its character, becoming vain as it is (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.26">De 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">Psa 115:8</reference>). A people's character never rises above that of its gods, which are its "better nature" [Bacon] (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.15">2Ki 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference>). <div eID="gen16852" type="x-p"/>
entries.365ff61657b620853356a7400d8d3852d51250f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9594"/><div sID="gen16853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9594"/><hi type="bold">6. Neither said they, Where, &c.--</hi>The very words which God uses (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">11, 13</reference>), when, as it were, reminding Himself of His former acts of love to Israel as a ground for interposing in their behalf again. When they would not say, Where is Jehovah, &c., God Himself at last said it for them (compare see on <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deserts ... pits--</hi>The desert between Mount Sinai and Palestine abounds in chasms and pits, in which beasts of burden often sink down to the knees. "Shadow of death" refers to the darkness of the caverns amidst the rocky precipices (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">De 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">32:10</reference>). <div eID="gen16854" type="x-p"/>
entries.df53b4094b73bc3b1e5756f72d348ae3505338c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9595"/><div sID="gen16855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9595"/><hi type="bold">7. plentiful--</hi>literally, "a land of Carmel," or "well-cultivated land": a garden land, in contrast to the "land of deserts" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled--</hi>by idolatries (<reference osisRef="Judg.2.10-Judg.2.17">Jud 2:10-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.58">Psa 78:58</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.59">59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">106:38</reference>).<div eID="gen16856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you ... ye--</hi>change to the second person from the third, "they" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>), in order to bring home the guilt to the living generation. <div eID="gen16857" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ccde096b49871e2fac7402e6a6e052eaabd91b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9596"/><div sID="gen16858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9596"/>8. The three leading classes, whose very office under the theocracy was to lead the people to God, disowned Him in the same language as the nation at large, "Where is the Lord?" (See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priests--</hi>whose office it was to expound the law (Mal <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2:6, 7</reference>).<div eID="gen16859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handle--</hi>are occupied with the law as the subject of their profession.<div eID="gen16860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pastors--</hi>civil, not religious: princes (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jr 3:15</reference>), whose duty it was to tend their people.<div eID="gen16861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophets--</hi>who should have reclaimed the people from their apostasy, encouraged them in it by pretended oracles from Baal, the Phoenician false god.<div eID="gen16862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Baal--</hi>in his name and by his authority (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">Jr 11:21</reference>).<div eID="gen16863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked after things ... not profit--</hi>answering to, "walked after vanity," that is, idols (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.5">Jr 2:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jr 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">Ha 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen16864" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddc9c5bbc3a3625614734ab4300a93515ada34e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9597"/><div sID="gen16865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9597"/><hi type="bold">9. yet plead--</hi>namely, by inflicting still further judgments on you.<div eID="gen16865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children's children--</hi>Three manuscripts and Jerome omit "children's"; they seem to have thought it unsuitable to read "children's children," when "children" had not preceded. But it is designedly so written, to intimate that the final judgment on the nation would be suspended for many generations [Horsley]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.35">Eze 20:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mi 6:2</reference>). <div eID="gen16866" type="x-p"/>
entries.79079d427719298d6bd170082850f699326000dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9598"/><div sID="gen16867" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9598"/><hi type="bold">10. pass over the isles--</hi>rather, "cross over to the isles."<div eID="gen16867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim ... Kedar--</hi>that is, the heathen nations, west and east. Go where you will, you cannot find an instance of any heathen nation forsaking their own for other gods. Israel alone does this. Yet the heathen gods are false gods; whereas Israel, in forsaking Me for other gods, forsake their "glory" for unprofitable idols.<div eID="gen16868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim--</hi>Cyprus, colonized by Phoenicians, who built in it the city of Citium, the modern Chitti. Then the term came to be applied to all maritime coasts of the Mediterranean, especially Greece (<reference osisRef="Num.24.24">Nu 24:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Is 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Da 11:30</reference>).<div eID="gen16869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kedar--</hi>descended from Ishmael; the Bedouins and Arabs, east of Palestine. <div eID="gen16870" type="x-p"/>
entries.47ea4476a7fbae2a2c9bea0f2e3b7171f425a2a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9599"/><div sID="gen16871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9599"/><hi type="bold">11. glory--</hi>Jehovah, the glory of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">Psa 106:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.23">Ro 1:23</reference>). The Shekinah, or cloud resting on the sanctuary, was the symbol of "the glory of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.11">1Ki 8:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>). The golden calf was intended as an image of the true God (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">Ex 32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.5">5</reference>), yet it is called an "idol" (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.41">Ac 7:41</reference>). It (like Roman Catholic images) was a violation of the second commandment, as the heathen multiplying of gods is a violation of the first.<div eID="gen16871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not profit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jr 2:8</reference>). <div eID="gen16872" type="x-p"/>
entries.799d36455939b2badacf15170a60adcb12b977f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9600"/><div sID="gen16873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9600"/>12. Impassioned personification (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horribly afraid--</hi>rather, be horrified."<div eID="gen16874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be ... very desolate--</hi>rather, "be exceedingly aghast" at the monstrous spectacle. Literally, "to be dried up," or "devastated," (places devastated have such an unsightly look) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen16875" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b2a397b8f51a3c2e8ca5197a580abd244ee1c3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9601"/><div sID="gen16876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9601"/><hi type="bold">13. two evils--</hi>not merely one evil, like the idolaters who know no better; besides simple idolatry, My people add the sin of forsaking the true God whom they have known; the heathen, though having the sin of idolatry, are free from the further sin of changing the true God for idols (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jr 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forsaken me--</hi>The Hebrew collocation brings out the only living God into more prominent contrast with idol nonentities. "Me they have forsaken, the Fountain," &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jr 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.14">Joh 4:14</reference>).<div eID="gen16877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broken cisterns--</hi>tanks for rain water, common in the East, where wells are scarce. The tanks not only cannot give forth an ever-flowing fresh supply as fountains can, but cannot even retain the water poured into them; the stonework within being broken, the earth drinks up the collected water. So, in general, all earthly, compared with heavenly, means of satisfying man's highest wants (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>, 2; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Lu 12:33</reference>). <div eID="gen16878" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2a55798b2c5d8d51bea0863e275096c7e3703c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9602"/><div sID="gen16879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9602"/><hi type="bold">14. is he a homeborn slave--</hi>No. "Israel is Jehovah's son, even His first-born" (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Ex 4:22</reference>). <reference osisRef="Jer.2.16">Jr 2:16</reference>, 18, 36, and the absence of any express contrast of the two parts of the nation are against Eichorn's view, that the prophet proposes to Judah, as yet spared, the case of Israel (the ten tribes) which had been carried away by Assyria as a warning of what they might expect if they should still put their trust in Egypt. "Were Israel's ten tribes of meaner birth than Judah? Certainly not. If, then, the former fell before Assyria, what can Judah hope from Egypt against Assyria? ... Israel" is rather here the whole of the remnant still left in their own land, that is, Judah. "How comes it to pass that the nation which once was under God's special protection (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jr 2:3</reference>) is now left at the mercy of the foe as a worthless slave?" The prophet sees this event as if present, though it was still future to Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen16879" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b78d6266b3220f93e646119b3b64ce076742f1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9603"/><div sID="gen16880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9603"/><hi type="bold">15. lions--</hi>the Babylonian princes (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jr 4:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Am 3:4</reference>). The disaster from the Babylonians in the fourth year of Jehoiakim's reign, and again three years later when, relying on Egypt, he revolted from Nebuchadnezzar, is here referred to (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>, 2). <div eID="gen16880" type="x-p"/>
entries.edaca4677816ca9d9f84ebd583e11bda9f039720: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9604"/><div sID="gen16881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9604"/><hi type="bold">16. Noph ... Tahapanes--</hi>Memphis, capital of Lower Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile, near the pyramids of Gizeh, opposite the site of modern Cairo. Daphne, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, near Pelusium, on the frontier of Egypt towards Palestine. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.4">Is 30:4</reference> contracts it, Hanes. These two cities, one the capital, the other that with which the Jews came most in contact, stand for the whole of Egypt. Tahapanes takes its name from a goddess, Tphnet [Champollion]. Memphis is from Man-nofri, "the abode of good men"; written in Hebrew, Moph (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.6">Ho 9:6</reference>), or Noph. The reference is to the coming invasion of Judah by Pharaoh-necho of Egypt, on his return from the Euphrates, when he deposed Jehoahaz and levied a heavy tribute on the land (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33-2Kgs.23.35">2Ki 23:33-35</reference>). Josiah's death in battle with the same Pharaoh is probably included (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen16881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have broken--</hi>rather, shall feed down the crown, &c., that is, affect with the greatest ignominy, such as baldness was regarded in the East (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jr 48:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.23">2Ki 2:23</reference>). Instead of "also," translate, "even" the Egyptians, in whom thou dost trust, shall miserably disappoint thy expectation [Maurer]. Jehoiakim was twice leagued with them (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">35</reference>): when he received the crown from them, and when he revolted from Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>, 2, 7). The Chaldeans, having become masters of Asia, threatened Egypt. Judea, situated between the contending powers, was thus exposed to the inroads of the one or other of the hostile armies; and unfortunately, except in Josiah's reign, took side with Egypt, contrary to God's warnings. <div eID="gen16882" type="x-p"/>
entries.211a844ca77f4c3887fdf7bf9f5b706f9d97a060: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9605"/><div sID="gen16883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9605"/>17. Literally, "Has not thy forsaking the Lord ... procured this (calamity) to thee?" So the Septuagint: the Masoretic accents make "this" the subject of the verb, leaving the object to be understood. "Has not this procured (it, that is, the impending calamity) unto thee, that hast forsaken?" &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.18">Jr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen16883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">led--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">De 32:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way--</hi>The article expresses the right way, the way of the Lord: namely, the moral training which they enjoyed in the Mosaic covenant. <div eID="gen16885" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d2efcf551bf871ec28e6c521c800ab4966468f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9606"/><div sID="gen16886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9606"/><hi type="bold">18. now--</hi>used in a reasoning sense, not of time.<div eID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way of Egypt--</hi>What hast thou to do with the way, that is, with going down to Egypt; or what ... with going to Assyria?<div eID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink ... waters--</hi>that is, to seek reinvigorating aid from them; so <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>, 36; compare "waters," meaning numerous forces (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>).<div eID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sihor--</hi>that is, the black river, in Greek, Melas ("black"), the Nile: so called from the black deposit or soil it leaves after the inundation (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Is 23:3</reference>). The Septuagint identifies it with Gihon, one of the rivers of Paradise.<div eID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the river--</hi>Euphrates, called by pre-eminence, the river; figurative for the Assyrian power. In 625 B.C., the seventeenth year of Josiah, and the fourth of Jeremiah's office, the kingdom of Assyria fell before Babylon, therefore Assyria is here put for Babylon its successor: so in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">La 5:6</reference>. There was doubtless a league between Judea and Assyria (that is, Babylon), which caused Josiah to march against Pharaoh-necho of Egypt when that king went against Babylon: the evil consequences of this league are foretold in this verse and <reference osisRef="Jer.2.36">Jr 2:36</reference>. <div eID="gen16890" type="x-p"/>
entries.201f5d217dc88beb1362fd7b9465446bc5612db7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9607"/><div sID="gen16891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9607"/><hi type="bold">19. correct ... reprove--</hi>rather, in the severer sense, "chastise ... punish" [Maurer].<div eID="gen16891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backslidings--</hi>"apostasies"; plural, to express the number and variety of their defections. The very confederacies they entered into were the occasion of their overthrow (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Is 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">Ho 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know ... see--</hi>imperative for futures: Thou shalt know and see to thy cost.<div eID="gen16893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my fear--</hi>rather, "the fear of Me." <div eID="gen16894" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ec8261cdbecc9962fa990949c84008a578b146b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9608"/><div sID="gen16895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9608"/><hi type="bold">20. I--</hi>the Hebrew should be pointed as the second person feminine, a form common in Jeremiah: "Thou hast broken," &c. So the Septuagint, and the sense requires it.<div eID="gen16895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy yoke ... bands--</hi>the yoke and bands which I laid on thee, My laws (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.5">Jr 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">transgress--</hi>so the Keri, and many manuscripts read. But the Septuagint and most authorities read, "I will not serve," that is, obey. The sense of English Version is, "I broke thy yoke (in Egypt)," &c., "and (at that time) thou saidst, I will not transgress; whereas thou hast (since then) wandered (from Me)" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">Ex 19:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hill ... green tree--</hi>the scene of idolatries (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.2">De 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.5">Is 57:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen16898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wanderest--</hi>rather, "thou hast bowed down thyself" (for the act of adultery: figurative of shameless idolatry, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.15">Ex 34:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.16">16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference>). <div eID="gen16899" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2feb448621fd6da88bacdf2e02bfbc41d159c73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9609"/><div sID="gen16900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9609"/>21. The same image as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">Psa 80:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen16900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>with respect to Me. <div eID="gen16901" type="x-p"/>
entries.6798a94920edf9863e296316ca86c23fdf2c355d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9610"/><div sID="gen16902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9610"/><hi type="bold">22. nitre--</hi>not what is now so called, namely, saltpeter; but the natron of Egypt, a mineral alkali, an incrustation at the bottom of the lakes, after the summer heat has evaporated the water: used for washing (compare <reference osisRef="Job.9.30">Job 9:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.20">Pr 25:20</reference>).<div eID="gen16902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soap--</hi>potash, the carbonate of which is obtained impure from burning different plants, especially the kali of Egypt and Arabia. Mixed with oil it was used for washing.<div eID="gen16903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">marked--</hi>deeply ingrained, indelibly marked; the Hebrew, catham, being equivalent to cathab. Others translate, "is treasured up," from the Arabic. Maurer from a Syriac root, "is polluted." <div eID="gen16904" type="x-p"/>
entries.8691383e0e3fc5604993774023d7cefe69f3e7b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9611"/><div sID="gen16905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9611"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.12">Pr 30:12</reference>).<div eID="gen16905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Baalim--</hi>plural, to express manifold excellency: compare Elohim.<div eID="gen16906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">see--</hi>consider.<div eID="gen16907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the valley--</hi>namely, of Hinnom, or Tophet, south and east of Jerusalem: rendered infamous by the human sacrifices to Moloch in it (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.19.2">Jr 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">6, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">32:35</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>).<div eID="gen16908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art--</hi>omit. The substantive that follows in this verse (and also that in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jr 2:24</reference>) is in apposition with the preceding "thou."<div eID="gen16909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dromedary--</hi>rather, a "young she-camel."<div eID="gen16910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">traversing--</hi>literally, "enfolding"; making its ways complicated by wandering hither and thither, lusting after the male. Compare as to the Jews' spiritual lust, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.6">Ho 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen16911" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae337bfce311af1cb4893ed0cf1cd433668ad5d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9612"/><div sID="gen16912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9612"/>24. (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.6">Jr 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.5">Job 39:5</reference>). "A wild ass," agreeing with "thou" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.23">Jr 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen16912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at her pleasure--</hi>rather, "in her ardor," namely, in pursuit of a male, sniffing the wind to ascertain where one is to be found [Maurer].<div eID="gen16913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occasion--</hi>either from a Hebrew root, "to meet"; "her meeting (with the male for sexual intercourse), who can avert it?" Or better from an Arabic root: "her heat (sexual impulse), who can allay it?" [Maurer].<div eID="gen16914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all they--</hi>whichever of the males desire her company [Horsley].<div eID="gen16915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will not weary themselves--</hi>have no need to weary themselves in searching for her.<div eID="gen16916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her month--</hi>in the season of the year when her sexual impulse is strongest, she puts herself in the way of the males, so that they have no difficulty in finding her. <div eID="gen16917" type="x-p"/>
entries.0515d7a8ac5fe7b3c6eeb88d1a318300d24f38fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9613"/><div sID="gen16918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9613"/><hi type="bold">25. Withhold, &c.--</hi>that is, abstain from incontinence; figuratively for idolatry [Houbigant].<div eID="gen16918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unshod, &c.--</hi>do not run so violently in pursuing lovers, as to wear out thy shoes: do not "thirst" so incontinently after sexual intercourse. Hitzig thinks the reference is to penances performed barefoot to idols, and the thirst occasioned by loud and continued invocations to them.<div eID="gen16919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no hope--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">Jr 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">Is 57:10</reference>). "It is hopeless," that is, I am desperately resolved to go on in my own course.<div eID="gen16920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>that is, laying aside the metaphor, "strange gods" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.13">Jr 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.16">De 32:16</reference>). <div eID="gen16921" type="x-p"/>
entries.385898aa26dfd18dbdfea34589734d7d4d5c7802: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9614"/><div sID="gen16922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9614"/><hi type="bold">26. is ashamed--</hi>is put to shame.<div eID="gen16922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thief--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.10.1">Joh 10:1</reference>).<div eID="gen16923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Israel--</hi>that is, Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.28">Jr 2:28</reference>). <div eID="gen16924" type="x-p"/>
entries.68411e61141e6e461f78b4709ba0e47a0558c328: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9615"/><div sID="gen16925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9615"/><hi type="bold">27. Thou art my father--</hi>(Contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">Jr 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">Is 64:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... trouble they will say--</hi>namely, to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Psa 78:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Is 26:16</reference>). Trouble often brings men to their senses (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.16-Luke.15.18">Lu 15:16-18</reference>). <div eID="gen16926" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ee74c2034dc316a7b0819e4499a784bc9695fed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9616"/><div sID="gen16927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9616"/><hi type="bold">28. But--</hi>God sends them to the gods for whom they forsook Him, to see if they can help them (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.37">De 32:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Jud 10:14</reference>).<div eID="gen16927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the number of thy cities--</hi>Besides national deities, each city had its tutelary god (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jr 11:13</reference>). <div eID="gen16928" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e4e3affaa67fb6b05fd7aac228d2c100c897f88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9617"/><div sID="gen16929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9617"/><hi type="bold">29. plead with me--</hi>that is, contend with Me for afflicting you (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.23">Jr 2:23</reference>, 35). <div eID="gen16929" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e9a2e14cf7c185d8faae15a119d7e77d6550a6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9618"/><div sID="gen16930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9618"/>30. (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.29">6:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Is 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">9:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your children--</hi>that is, your people, you.<div eID="gen16931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your ... sword ... devoured ... prophets--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2Ch 36:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.26">Ne 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.29">Mt 23:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.31">31</reference>). <div eID="gen16932" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcddeb7594ecdea3a9b167ef5b84b727c25edd3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9619"/><div sID="gen16933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9619"/>31. The Hebrew collocation is, "O, the generation, ye," that is, "O ye who now live." The generation needed only to be named, to call its degeneracy to view, so palpable was it.<div eID="gen16933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilderness--</hi>in which all the necessaries of life are wanting. On the contrary, Jehovah was a never-failing source of supply for all Israel's wants in the wilderness, and afterwards in Canaan.<div eID="gen16934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>literally, "darkness of Jehovah," the strongest Hebrew term for "darkness; the densest darkness"; compare "land of the shadow of death" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We are lords--</hi>that is, We are our own masters. We will worship what gods we like (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">Psa 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">82:6</reference>). But it is better to translate from a different Hebrew root: "We ramble at large," without restraint pursuing our idolatrous lusts. <div eID="gen16936" type="x-p"/>
entries.2561bda399012b0e7501659795cd555b2edc1d9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9620"/><div sID="gen16937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9620"/>32. Oriental women greatly pride themselves on their ornaments (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">attire--</hi>girdles for the breast.<div eID="gen16938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgotten me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.13.25">Jr 13:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">Ho 8:14</reference>). <div eID="gen16939" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8ac68391c043e9980d83d3c9ee99f5ab2d33d5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9621"/><div sID="gen16940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9621"/><hi type="bold">33. Why trimmest--</hi>Maurer translates, "How skilfully thou dost prepare thy way," &c. But see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.30">2Ki 9:30</reference>. "Trimmest" best suits the image of one decking herself as a harlot.<div eID="gen16940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">way--</hi>course of life.<div eID="gen16941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>accordingly. Or else, "nay, thou hast even," &c.<div eID="gen16942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also ... wicked ones--</hi>even the wicked harlots, that is, (laying aside the metaphor) even the Gentiles who are wicked, thou teachest to be still more so [Grotius]. <div eID="gen16943" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb60e0d47bae271604615dbc80f765763e9ce65d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9622"/><div sID="gen16944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9622"/><hi type="bold">34. Also--</hi>not only art thou polluted with idolatry, but also with the guilt of shedding innocent blood [Maurer]. Rosenmuller not so well translates, "even in thy skirts," &c.; that is, there is no part of thee (not even thy skirts) that is not stained with innocent blood (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jr 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.16">2Ki 21:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">Psa 106:38</reference>). See as to innocent blood shed, not as here in honor of idols, but of prophets for having reproved them (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.30">Jr 2:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.23">Jr 26:20-23</reference>).<div eID="gen16944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">souls--</hi>that is, persons.<div eID="gen16945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">search--</hi>I did not need to "search deep" to find proof of thy guilt; for it was "upon all these" thy skirts. Not in deep caverns didst thou perpetrate these atrocities, but openly in the vale of Hinnom and within the precincts of the temple. <div eID="gen16946" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fe68ad80e3b52e04f2db82a9e5960119790e0a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9623"/><div sID="gen16947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9623"/>35. (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.23">Jr 2:23</reference>, 29). <div eID="gen16947" type="x-p"/>
entries.7eafdaedf3bb676dad1baa457fe426a08126bdcd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9624"/><div sID="gen16948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9624"/><hi type="bold">36. gaddest--</hi>runnest to and fro, now seeking help from Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.16-2Chr.28.21">2Ch 28:16-21</reference>), now from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">Jr 37:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.3">Is 30:3</reference>). <div eID="gen16948" type="x-p"/>
entries.e52a3ca898a74c6bd0bf8eecc3a40d0ff6af70c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9625"/><div sID="gen16949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9625"/><hi type="bold">37. him--</hi>Egypt.<div eID="gen16949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hands upon ... head--</hi>expressive of mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.19">2Sa 13:19</reference>).<div eID="gen16950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in them--</hi>in those stays in which thou trustest. <chapter eID="Jer.2"/>

entries.9a33569c4ade64c5128b5e4d0278ec6e43599b33: <div eID="gen29192" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29193" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29194" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29194" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29193" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29195" type="x-p"/> God expresses his continued regard for his people, long since chosen, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.1-Jer.2.3">Jer 2:1-3</reference>. He then expostulates with them on their ungrateful and worse than heathen return to his regard, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.4-Jer.2.11">Jer 2:4-11</reference>; at which even the inanimate creation must be astonished, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.12">Jer 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jer 2:13</reference>. After this their guilt is declared to be the sole cause of the calamities which their enemies had power to inflict on them, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.14-Jer.2.17">Jer 2:14-17</reference>. They are upbraided for their alliances with idolatrous countries, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jer 2:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jer 2:19</reference>; and for their strong propensity to idolatry, notwithstanding all the care and tender mercy of God, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20-Jer.2.29">Jer 2:20-29</reference>. Even the chastenings of the Almighty have produced in this people no repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.30">Jer 2:30</reference>. The chapter concludes with compassionately remonstrating against their folly and ingratitude in revolting so deeply from God, and with warning them of the fearful consequences, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jer 2:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.37">Jer 2:37</reference>.
entries.d569218902124d772885b8106c3ba50d607d40fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29196" type="x-p"/> I remember thee - The youth here refers to their infant political state when they came out of Egypt; they just then began to be a people. Their espousals refer to their receiving the law at Mount Sinai, which they solemnly accepted, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.6-Exo.24.8">Exo 24:6-8</reference>, and which acceptance was compared to a betrothing or espousal. Previously to this they were no people, for they had no constitution nor form of government. When they received the law, and an establishment in the Promised Land, then they became a people and a nation. <div eID="gen29196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29197" type="x-p"/> Wentest after me - Receivedst my law, and wert obedient to it; confiding thyself wholly to my guidance, and being conscientiously attached to my worship. The kindness was that which God showed them by taking them to be his people, not their kindness to him.
entries.daaaf41b0de2a726a29e7860a8d0cddadf806b96: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29198" type="x-p"/> Israel was holiness unto the Lord - Fully consecrated to his service. <div eID="gen29198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29199" type="x-p"/> The first fruits of his increase - They were as wholly the Lord's, as the first fruits were the property of the priests according to the law <reference osisRef="Num.18.13">Num 18:13</reference>. These the priests alone had a right to devote to their own use. <div eID="gen29199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29200" type="x-p"/> All that devour him shall offend - As they were betrothed to the Lord, they were considered his especial property; they therefore who injured them were considered as laying violent hands on the property of God. They who persecute God's children have a grievous burden to bear, an awful account to give.
entries.e907e08e441cf8777081f5f8897287f41033e796: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29201" type="x-p"/> What iniquity have your fathers found in me - Have they ever discovered any thing cruel, unjust, oppressive in my laws? Any thing unkind or tyrannical in my government? Why then have they become idolaters?
entries.55d6ea32c2baed0c2b88d0169dd2c36573a0259e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29202" type="x-p"/> Through the wilderness - Egypt was the house of their bondage: the desert through which they passed after they came out of Egypt, was a place where the means of life were not to be found; where no one family could subsist, much less a company of 600, 000 men. God mentions these things to show that it was by the bounty of an especial providence that they were fed and preserved alive. Previously to this, it was a land through which no man passed, and in which no man dwelt. And why? because it did not produce the means of life; it was the shadow of death in its appearance, and the grave to those who committed themselves to it.
entries.1488e7f36850b9d5021b70b756d67338cf34ad96: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29203" type="x-p"/> And I brought you into a plentiful country - The land of Canaan. <div eID="gen29203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29204" type="x-p"/> My land - The particular property of God, which he gave to them as an inheritance, they being his peculiar people.
entries.f3e01ef78a1b76ada02ce3d8826b20e1b7e442d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29205" type="x-p"/> They that handle the law - ותפשי vethophe shey, they that draw out the law; they whose office it is to explain it, draw out its spiritual meanings, and show to what its testimonies refer. <div eID="gen29205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29206" type="x-p"/> The pastors also - Kings, political and civil rulers. <div eID="gen29206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29207" type="x-p"/> Prophesied by Baal - Became his prophets, and were inspired with the words of lying spirits.
entries.45fcec4c61d4bcc16a7f33851fe02142b1aff74c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29208" type="x-p"/> I will yet plead with you - אריב arib, I will maintain my process, vindicate my own conduct, and prove the wickedness of yours.
entries.c584913563efeaeac10128ec49426bcaf5bae780: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29209" type="x-p"/> The isles of Chittim - This is the island of Cyprus, according to Josephus. In 1 Maccabees 8:5, it is taken for Macedonia. Besides this, how they (the Romans) had discomfited in battle Philip and Perseus, king of the Chittims. Chittim was the grandson of Japhet; and Bochart has made it appear that the countries inhabited by the Chittim were Italy and the adjacent provinces of Europe, lying along the coast of the Mediterranean Sea; and probably this is the prophet's meaning. <div eID="gen29209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29210" type="x-p"/> Send unto Kedar - The name of an Arabian tribe. See if nations either near or remote, cultivated or stupid, have acted with such fickleness and ingratitude as you have done! They have retained their gods to whom they had no obligation; ye have abandoned your God, to whom ye owe your life, breath, and all things!
entries.5a2d14195116eacd12dc800a6ce251c899c37bb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29211" type="x-p"/> Be astonished, O ye heavens - Or, the heavens are astonished. The original will admit either sense. The conduct of this people was so altogether bad, that among all the iniquities of mankind, neither heaven nor earth had witnessed any thing so excessively sinful and profligate.
entries.d2edf1734f0705b60e011fb6949d9e7ec176edca: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29212" type="x-p"/> Two evils - First, they forsook God, the Fountain of life, light, prosperity, and happiness. Secondly, they hewed out broken cisterns; they joined themselves to idols, from whom they could receive neither temporal nor spiritual good! Their conduct was the excess of folly and blindness. What we call here broken cisterns, means more properly such vessels as were ill made, not staunch, ill put together, so that the water leaked through them.
entries.529e419d17148f87e132aed15d7aee8fcd43232b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29213" type="x-p"/> Is Israel a servant? - Is he a slave purchased with money, or a servant born in the family? He is a son himself. If so, then, why is he spoiled? Not because God has not shown him love and kindness; but because he forsook God, turned to and is joined with idols.
entries.593c73c4808346edb768307492e93622532f9453: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29214" type="x-p"/> The young lions roared upon him - The Assyrians, who have sacked and destroyed the kingdom of Israel, with a fierceness like that of pouncing upon their prey.
entries.1c47ce09638b00954c94cb6e1873b6a4f1855e5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29215" type="x-p"/> The children of Noph and Tahapanes - Noph and Tahapanes were two cities of Egypt, otherwise called Memphis and Daphni. It is well known that the good king was defeated by the Egyptians, and slain in battle. Thus was the crown of Judah's head broken.
entries.db8300ede52fb0603b90f33ad1815d46e9179f3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29216" type="x-p"/> What hast thou to do in the way of Egypt - Why dost thou make alliances with Egypt? <div eID="gen29216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29217" type="x-p"/> To drink the waters of Sihor? - This means the Nile. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Isa 23:3</reference> (note). <div eID="gen29217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29218" type="x-p"/> The way of Assyria - Why make alliances with the Assyrians? All such connections will only expedite thy ruin. <div eID="gen29218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29219" type="x-p"/> To drink the waters of the river? - The Euphrates, as נהר nahar or הנהר hannahar always means Euphrates, the country between the Tigris and Euphrates, is termed to this day Maher alnahar, "the country beyond the river," i.e., Mesopotamia. <div eID="gen29219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29220" type="x-p"/> Instead of cleaving to the Lord, they joined affinity and made alliances with those two nations, who were ever jealous of them, and sought their ruin. Egypt was to them a broken reed instead of a staff; Assyria was a leaky cistern, from which they could derive no help.
entries.1bfa5437f2bed44ac976305d55acb6113878ed70: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29221" type="x-p"/> Of old time I have broken thy yoke - It is thought by able critics that the verbs should be read in the second person singular, Thou hast broken thy yoke, Thou hast burst thy bonds; and thus the Septuagint, συνετριψας τον ζυγον σου, "thou hast broken thy yoke." And the Vulgate, Confregisti jugum meum, rupisti, vincula mea; "Thou hast broken my yoke; thou hast burst my bonds;" and so the Arabic. But the Chaldee gives it a meaning which removes the difficulty: "I have broken the yoke of the people from thy neck; I have cut your bonds asunder." And when this was done, they did promise fair: for "thou saidst, I will not transgress;" but still they played the harlot - committed idolatrous acts in the high places, where the heathen had built their altars, pretending that elevation of this kind assisted their devotion.
entries.2e3532f7052ebf393103b107665cb7ca9fdd9eaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29222" type="x-p"/> I had planted thee a noble vine - I gave thee the fullest instruction, the purest ordinances, the highest privileges; and reason would that I should expect thee to live suitably to such advantages; but instead of this thou art become degenerate; the tree is deteriorated, and the fruit is bad. Instead of being true worshippers, and of a holy life and conversation, ye are become idolaters of the most corrupt and profligate kind. See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>, etc., where the same image is used.
entries.31fd563285c92b4acd5827070db98bce266bcd0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen29222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29223" type="x-p"/> For though thou wash thee with nitre - It should be rendered natar or natron, a substance totally different from our nitre. It comes from the root נתר nathar, to dissolve, loosen, because a solution of it in water is abstersive, taking out spots, etc., from clothes. It is still used in the east for the purpose of washing. If vinegar be poured on it, Dr. Shaw says, a strong effervescence is the immediate consequence, which illustrates <reference osisRef="Pro.25.20">Pro 25:20</reference> : "The singing of songs to a heavy heart is like vinegar upon natron;" that is, there is no affinity between them; opposition and strife are occasioned by any attempt to unite them. <div eID="gen29223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29224" type="x-p"/> Thine iniquity is marked before me - No washing will take out thy spots; the marks of thy idolatry and corruption are too deeply rooted to be extracted by any human means.
entries.d44a3f37068b09f94ec531db250907a5519670fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen29224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29225" type="x-p"/> See thy way in the valley - The valley of Hinnom, where they offered their own children to Moloch, an idol of the Ammonites. <div eID="gen29225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29226" type="x-p"/> A swift dromedary traversing her ways - Dr. Blayney translates, "A fleet dromedary that hath taken to company with her." Dr. Dahler rather paraphrases, thus: - <div eID="gen29226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29227" type="x-p"/> Semblable a une dromedaire en chaleur, <div eID="gen29227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29228" type="x-p"/> Qui court d'une tote a l'autre. "Like to a dromedary in her desire for the male, <div eID="gen29228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29229" type="x-p"/> Which runs hither and thither." <div eID="gen29229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29230" type="x-p"/> This is an energetic comparison; and shows the unbridled attachment of those bad people to idolatry, and the abominable practices by which it was usually accompanied.
entries.6dca7dab3d08d60e3862c3f20f08b942a830c8ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen29230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29231" type="x-p"/> A wild ass used to the wilderness - Another comparison to express the same thing. <div eID="gen29231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29232" type="x-p"/> Snuffeth up the wind - In a high fever from the inward heat felt at such times, these animals open their mouths and nostrils as wide as possible, to take in large draughts of fresh air, in order to cool them. <div eID="gen29232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29233" type="x-p"/> In her mouth they shall find her - The meaning is, that although such animals are exceedingly fierce and dangerous when they are in this state; yet, as soon as they have found the male, the desire is satisfied, and they become quiet and governable as before. But it was not so with this idolatrous people: their desires were ever fierce and furious; they were never satiated, one indulgence always leading to an other. The brute beasts had only a short season in which this appetite prevailed; but they acted without restraint or limit.
entries.3e8cf546b6e8fd42fa7d19ba5411201fb517aef1: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen29233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29234" type="x-p"/> Withhold thy foot from being unshod - When it was said to them, "Cease from discovering thy feet; prostitute thyself no more to thy idols." <div eID="gen29234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29235" type="x-p"/> And thy throat from thirst - Drink no more of their libations, nor use those potions which tend only to increase thy appetite for pollution. Thou didst say, There is no hope: it is useless to advise me thus; I am determined; I have loved these strange pods, and to them will I cleave.
entries.70f7a15357c82368109b8707561c402c7029a7a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen29235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29236" type="x-p"/> As the thief is ashamed - As the pilferer is confounded when he is caught in the fact; so shalt thou, thy kings, princes, priests, and prophets, be confounded, when God shall arrest thee in thy idolatries, and deliver thee into the hands of thine enemies.
entries.9e1baba125558566693f4bb40d89f73f93cc9883: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen29236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29237" type="x-p"/> Thou art my father - By thee we have been produced, and by thee we are sustained. This was the property of the true God; for he is the Author and Supporter of being. How deeply fallen and brutishly ignorant must they be when they could attribute this to the stock of a tree!
entries.969224241056e7752825fbf6a7a8162212cf0e71: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen29237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29238" type="x-p"/> According to the number of thy cities are thy gods - Among heathen nations every city had its tutelary deity. Judah, far sunk in idolatry, had adopted this custom. The Church of Rome has refined it a little: every city has its tutelary saint, and this saint has a procession and worship peculiar to himself. So here; not much of the old idolatry is lost.
entries.bd34292bf944c4e59e0459881771c6b32fe48ccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen29238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29239" type="x-p"/> Have I been a wilderness unto Israel? - Have I ever withheld from you any of the blessings necessary for your support? <div eID="gen29239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29240" type="x-p"/> A land of darkness - Have you, since you passed through the wilderness, and came out of the darkness of Egypt, ever been brought into similar circumstances? You have had food and all the necessaries of life for your bodies; and my ordinances and word to enlighten and cheer your souls. I have neither been a wilderness nor a land of darkness to you. <div eID="gen29240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29241" type="x-p"/> We are lords - We wish to be our own masters; we will neither brook religious nor civil restraint; we will regard no laws, human or Divine. It was this disposition that caused them to fall in so fully with the whole system of idolatry.
entries.42ef69f3734af1825807877535a233349251a006: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen29241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29242" type="x-p"/> Can a maid forget her ornaments - This people has not so much attachment to me as young females have to their dress and ornaments. They never forget them and even when arrived at old age, look with pleasure on the dress and ornaments which they have worn in their youth. <div eID="gen29242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29243" type="x-p"/> Days without number - That is, for many years; during the whole reign of Manasses, which was fifty-five years, the land was deluged with idolatry, from which the reform by good King Josiah his grandson had not yet purified it.
entries.f67edfcf0a16212dfd1a749940e275c2e7c5775e: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen29243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29244" type="x-p"/> Why trimmest thou thy way - Ye have used a multitude of artifices to gain alliances with the neighboring idolatrous nations. <div eID="gen29244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29245" type="x-p"/> Hast thou also taught the wicked ones thy ways - Ye have made even these idolaters worse than they were before. Dr. Blayney translates, "Therefore have I taught calamity thy ways." A prosopopoeia: "I have instructed calamity where to find thee." Thou shalt not escape punishment.
entries.9f8b16c7826d1411b3f5d9e2d64366dd299cab10: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen29245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29246" type="x-p"/> The blood of the souls of the poor innocents - We find from the sacred history that Manasseh had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.16">2Kgs 21:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.34.10">Eze 34:10</reference>. <div eID="gen29246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29247" type="x-p"/> I have not found it by secret search, but upon all these - Such deeds of darkness and profligacy are found only in Israel. Dr. Blayney translates, "I have not found it in a digged hole, but upon every oak." Others cover the blood that it may not appear; but ye have shed it openly, and sprinkled it upon your consecrated oaks, and gloried in it.
entries.18f480579b93fa5271c4a0e4d718953523b69443: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen29247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29248" type="x-p"/> Because I am innocent - They continued to assert their innocence, and therefore expected that God's judgments would be speedily removed! <div eID="gen29248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29249" type="x-p"/> I will plead with thee - I will maintain my process, follow it up to conviction, and inflict the deserved punishment.
entries.aa6819a9eca9e3f344452a3de2c360eba816dcee: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen29249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29250" type="x-p"/> Why gaddest thou about - When they had departed from the Lord, they sought foreign alliances for support. <div eID="gen29250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29251" type="x-p"/> 1. The Assyrians <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.13-2Chr.28.21">2Chr 28:13-21</reference>; but they injured instead of helping them. <div eID="gen29251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29252" type="x-p"/> 2. The Egyptians: but in this they were utterly disappointed, and were ashamed of their confidence. <div eID="gen29252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29253" type="x-p"/> See <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7-Jer.37.8">Jer 37:7-8</reference> (note), for the fulfillment of this prediction.
entries.8ac0186d76b4bf741a854b4c8ff3481e616a363f: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen29253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29254" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt go forth from him, and thine hands upon thine head - Thou shalt find all thy confidence in vain, - thy hope disappointed; - and thy state reduced to desperation. The hand being placed on the head was the evidence of deep sorrow, occasioned by utter desolation. See the case of Tamar, when ruined and abandoned by her brother Amnon, <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.19">2Sam 13:19</reference>. <div eID="gen29254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29255" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not prosper in them - They shall all turn to thy disadvantage; and this as we shall see in the history of this people, was literally fulfilled. O what a grievous and bitter thing it is to sin against the Lord, and have him for an enemy!  <chapter eID="Jer.2"/> <div eID="gen29255" type="x-p"/>

entries.8e3cc2b08d4b249a51079286e8013dbb7d88cde4: <div eID="gen13763" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">I. General Admonitions and Reproofs Belonging to the Time of Josiah - Jeremiah 2-22</title> <div sID="gen13764" type="x-p"/> If we compare the six longer discourses in these chapters with the sayings and prophecies gathered together in the other portions of the book, we observe between them this distinction in form and matter, that the former are more <hi type="italic">general</hi> in their character than the latter. Considered as to their form, these last prophecies have, with few exceptions, headings in which we are told both the date of their composition and the circumstances under which they were uttered; while in the headings of these six discourses, if we except the somewhat indefinite notice, "in the days of Josiah" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer 3:6</reference>), we find nowhere mentioned either their date or the circumstances which led to their composition. Again, both the shorter sayings and the lengthier prophecies between <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:1-14</reference> and the end of the book are unmistakeably to be looked upon as prophetic addresses, separately rounded off; but the discourses of our first part give us throughout the impression that they are not discourses delivered before the people, but treatises compiled in writing from the oral addresses of the prophet. As to their matter, too, we cannot fail to notice the difference that, whereas from <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:1-14</reference> onwards the king of Babylon is named as the executor of judgment upon Judah and the nations, in the discourses of <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jer 2-20</reference> the enemies who are to execute judgment are nowhere defined, but are only generally described as a powerful and terrible nation coming from the north. And so, in rebuking the idolatry and the prevailing sins of the people, no reference is made to special contemporary events; but there are introduced to a great extent lengthy general animadversions on their moral degeneracy, and reflections on the vanity if idolatry and the nature of true wisdom. From these facts we infer the probable conclusion that these discourses are but comprehensive summaries of the prophet’s labours in the days of Josiah. The probability becomes certainty when we perceive that the matters treated in these discourses are arranged according to their subjects. The first discourse (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.1-Jer.3.5">Jer 2:1-3:5</reference>) gives, so to speak, the programme of the subjects of all the following discourses: that disloyal defection to idolatry, with which Israel has from of old requited the Lord for His love and faithfulness, brings with it sore chastening judgments. In the second discourse (Jer 3:6-6:30) faithless Judah is shown, in the fall of the ten tribes, what awaits itself in case of stiff-necked persistence in idolatry. In the third (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">Jer 7-10</reference>) is torn from it the support of a vain confidence in the possession of the temple and in the offering of the sacrifices commanded by the law. In the fourth (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jer 11-13</reference>) its sins are characterized as a breach of the covenant; and rejection by the Lord is declared to be its punishment. In the fifth (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.17">Jer 14-17</reference>) the hope is destroyed that the threatened chastisement can be turned aside by intercession. Finally, in the sixth (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">Jer 18-20</reference>) the judgment of the destruction of Jerusalem and of the kingdom of Judah is exhibited in symbolical acts. In this arrangement and distribution of what the prophet had to announce to the people in his endeavours to save them, if possible, from destruction, we can recognise a progression from general admonitions and threatenings to more and more definite announcement of coming judgments; and when, on the other hand, we see growing greater and bitterer the prophet’s complaints against the hatreds and persecutions he has to endure (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.6">Jer 12:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10-Jer.15.11">Jer 15:10-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.15-Jer.15.21">Jer 15:15-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.14-Jer.17.18">Jer 17:14-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18-Jer.18.23">Jer 18:18-23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">Jer 18:20</reference>), we can gather that the expectation of the people’s being saved from impending destruction was growing less and less, that their obduracy was increasing, and that judgment must inevitably come upon them. These complaints of the prophet cease with Jer 20, though later he had much fiercer hatred to endure. <div eID="gen13764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13765" type="x-p"/> None of these discourses contains any allusions to events that occurred after Josiah’s death, or stand in any relation to such events. Hence we believe we are safe in taking them for a digest of the quintessence of Jeremiah’s oral preaching in the days of Josiah, and this arranged with reference to the subject-matter. It was by this preaching that Jeremiah sought to give a firm footing to the king’s reformatory efforts to restore and inspire new life into the public worship, and to develope the external return to the legal temple worship into an inward conversion to the living God. And it was thus he sought, while the destruction of the kingdom was impending, to save all that would let themselves be saved; knowing as he did that God, in virtue of His unchangeable covenant faithfulness, would sharply chastise His faithless people for its obstinate apostasy from Him, but had not determined to make an utter end of it. <div eID="gen13765" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love and Faithfulness of the Lord, and Israel’s Disloyalty and Idolatry - Jeremiah 2:1-3:5</title> <div sID="gen13766" type="x-p"/> The Lord has loved Israel sincerely (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2-Jer.2.3">Jer 2:2-3</reference>), but Israel has fallen from the Lord its God and followed after imaginary gods (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.4-Jer.2.8">Jer 2:4-8</reference>); therefore He will yet further punish it for this unparalleled sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.9-Jer.2.19">Jer 2:9-19</reference>). From of old Israel has been renegade, and has by its idolatry contracted fearful guilt, being led not even by afflictions to return to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.20-Jer.2.30">Jer 2:20-30</reference>); therefore must the Lord chastise (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.31-Jer.2.37">Jer 2:31-37</reference>), because they will not repent (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.1-Jer.3.5">Jer 3:1-5</reference>). This discourse is of a quite general character; it only sketches the main thoughts which are extended in the following discourses and prophecies concerning Judah. So that by most critics it is held to be the discourse by which Jeremiah inaugurated his ministry; for, as Hitzig puts it, "in its finished completeness it gives the impression of a first-uttered outpouring of the heart, in which are set forth, without restraint, Jahveh’s list of grievances against Israel, which has long been running up." It unquestionably contains the chief of the thoughts uttered by the prophet at the beginning of his ministry. <div eID="gen13766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13767" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.1-Jer.2.3">Jer 2:1-3</reference> "<hi type="italic">And then came to me the word of Jahveh, saying: Go and publish in the ears of Jerusalem, saying: I have remembered to thy account the love of thy youth, the lovingness of thy courtship time, thy going after me in the wilderness, in a land unsown. Holy was Israel to the Lord, his first-fruits of the produce: all who would have devoured him brought guilt upon themselves: evil came upon him, is the saying of Jahveh</hi>." The <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jer 2:3</reference> are not "in a certain sense the text of the following reproof" (Graf), but contain "the main idea which shows the cause of the following rebuke" (Hitz.): The Lord has rewarded the people of Israel with blessings for its love to Him. זכר with ל pers. and accus. rei means: to remember to one’s account that it may stand him in good stead afterwards - cf. <reference osisRef="Neh.5.19">Neh 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.22">Neh 13:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.31">Neh 13:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.3">Psa 98:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>, etc. - that it may be repaid with evil, <reference osisRef="Neh.6.14">Neh 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.29">Neh 13:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference>, etc. The perfect זכרתּי is to be noted, and not inverted into the present. It is a thing completed that is spoken of; what the Lord has done, not what He is going on with. He remembered to the people Israel the love of its youth. חסד, ordinarily, condescending love, graciousness and favour; here, the self-devoting, nestling love of Israel to its God. The youth of Israel is the time of the sojourn in Egypt and of the Exodus thence (Hos 2:17; Hos 11:1); here the latter, as is shown by the following: lovingness of the courtship. The courtship comprises the time from the Exodus out of Egypt till the concluding of the covenant at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.8">Exo 19:8</reference>). When the Lord redeemed Israel with a strong hand out of the power of Egypt, He chose it to be His spouse, whom He bare on eagles’ wings and brought unto Himself, Exo 19:4. The love of the bride to her Lord and Husband, Israel proved by its following Him as He went before in the wilderness, the land where it is not sown, i.e., followed Him gladly into the parched, barren wilderness. "Thy going after me" is decisive for the question so much debated by commentators, whether חסד and אהבה stand for the love of Israel to its God, or God’s love to Israel. The latter view we find so early as Chrysostom, and still in Rosenm. and Graf; but it is entirely overthrown by the לכתּך  אחרי, which Chrysost. transforms into ποιῆσας ἐξακολουθῆσαι μου, while Graf takes no notice of it. The reasons, too, which Graf, after the example of Rosenm. and Dathe, brings in support of this and against the only feasible exposition, are altogether valueless. The assertion that the facts forbid us to understand the words of the love of Israel to the Lord, because history represents the Israelites, when <hi type="italic">vixdum Aegypto egressos, as refractarios et ad aliorum deorum cultum pronos</hi>, cannot be supported by a reference to <reference osisRef="Deut.9.6">Deu 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.24">Deu 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa 48:8</reference>; Amo 5:25., Psa 106:7. History knows of no apostasy of Israel from its God and no idolatry of the people during the time from the Exodus out of Egypt till the arrival at Sinai, and of this time alone Jeremiah speaks. All the rebellions of Israel against its God fall within the time after the conclusion of the covenant at Sinai, and during the march from Sinai to Canaan. On the way from Egypt to Sinai the people murmured repeatedly, indeed, against Moses; at the Red Sea, when Pharaoh was pursuing with chariots and horsemen (Exo 14:11.); at Marah, where they were not able to drink the water for bitterness (15:24); in the wilderness of Sin, for lack of bread and meat (Jer 16:2.); and at Massah, for want of water (Jer 17:2.). But in all these cases the murmuring was no apostasy from the Lord, no rebellion against God, but an outburst of timorousness and want of proper trust in God, as is abundantly clear from the fact that in all these cases of distress and trouble God straightway brings help, with the view of strengthening the confidence of the timorous people in the omnipotence of His helping grace.
